runs.text: Obra, ou trafego como de ſemear, re-

lines.note: Someqi denotes work or busy activity, illustrated by sowing and harvesting. The damaged headword is supported by the preceding page's clear catchword; Obra and the final re- replace the provisional garbling.
Completes recolher fruito, gathering the crop. The final upright S marks written usage and is separated from the italic Portuguese gloss.

runs.text: Some çuqe. i, Yeno aru chauan, ſara.

lines.note: Sometsuke is paraphrased as cups or dishes bearing pictures. The print spaces Some çuqe; the Portuguese word for porcelain starts at the right edge.

runs.text: ſolana, ou bacios da China pintados.

lines.note: Completes the historical Por-solana spelling and adds painted Chinese bowls. The crop supports bacios rather than OCR hacios; the source spelling is not normalized to porcelana.
Somi/somu means becoming dyed or affected by something. Iro ni somi begins an example of attraction to what one sees, continued by a parallel phrase below.

Ka ni mezuru completes the Japanese pairing of attraction to colour and fragrance. The Portuguese describes immediate attachment or desire; cobiçar is printed with the historical initial cu- and divided after cubi-.
Completes desiring what one sees, then gives chi ni somu, being stained in blood. The visible Chini replaces provisional Cuini; the literal dyeing gloss begins anew.
Completes tingir-se and translates the example as being dyed or bathed in blood. It is the literal counterpart to the preceding attraction example.
Somikaeri describes being deeply or thoroughly stained. The visible mi and the matching example below correct provisional Sonicayeri without changing the historical principal parts.
Ake no chishio ni somikaetta describes being drenched in red blood. The worn q and e in Aqeno are read with the surviving strokes and blood context; the Portuguese tinto continues below.
Completes tinto, saying the subject became stained and bathed in blood. The phrase directly confirms the intensive dyeing sense of the headword.
Somin is paraphrased as rough common people and glossed as country folk. The crop supports Gente rather than Geme, and the second occurrence is abbreviated and divided as gẽ-.
Completes gente rustica e baixa, rural people of low social standing in the dictionary's wording. Baixa is wholly italic and ends with a period, not the provisional mixed-font hyphen.
Sominarai means learning or acquiring habits by association. The headword begins S, not OCR B; Aprender is visible, and Fi- starts hito across the row boundary.

runs.text: toto aitomoni vorutoqi ba, jinenni ſomi-

lines.note: Completes hito to aitomoni oru toki ba: while staying together with a person, one naturally learns their habits. The initial j of jinenni is damaged but present; sominaroo continues below.

runs.text: Aprender, ou tomar os cuſtumes da

lines.note: Completes sominaroo and starts the explanation of learning or taking on another person's customs. The printed r and caron replace OCR natǒ; cuſtumes retains the visible historical vowel.

runs.text: peßoa com quem ſe conuerſa, ou eſtà.

lines.note: Completes the account of acquiring the habits of the person with whom one associates or stays. The reflexive phrase describes companionship rather than conversation alone.
Soomyoo, paraphrased soo no na, is a common or general name. The Portuguese definition and the printed circumflex/caron combination distinguish this from nearby homographs.
Completes the definition as the general name of a thing. The final consonant of geral is l, not the provisional i.
Soomoku is vegetation, paraphrased kusa and ki: herbs or grasses and trees. Both parts of the Sino-Japanese compound receive explicit vernacular equivalents.
Somoodo is identified with somabito, the timber worker already defined on f444. The damaged synonym is read as Somabito, not the provisional Sumrabito; the Portuguese clause continues below.
Completes the description of a man who prepares or cuts timber in the woods. The final phrase confirms the occupational reading of Somabito.

runs.text: Porta principal por onde todos, ou

lines.note: Soomon here is the principal gate used by everyone. The collective sense is developed in the next row rather than specifying an exclusively ceremonial entrance.

runs.text: toda aſorte de gente entra, & ſaye.

lines.note: Completes the gate definition: people of every kind enter and leave through it. Toda replaces OCR tada, while the close printed aſorte spacing is retained.
The second Soomon denotes addressing the ruler. The crop reads ao Rey rather than provisional co Rey, and Rey is wholly italic; the Japanese example continues on the short next row.
Moosu completes soomon moosu, respectfully making an address or report to the ruler. The independent physical row is preserved despite its brevity.

Somosomo is paraphrased sate mata and initially glossed as moreover or consequently. The visible second o corrects provisional Somoſumo; second-pass enlargement identifies the double-s ligature in dißo, rather than two tall ſ-types.

runs.text: conſequente mente. ¶ Itẽ, Palaura com que

lines.note: Completes the connective gloss, then introduces a second use as an opening word. The source spaces consequente mente and abbreviates Item; Palaura corrects OCR Palhura.

runs.text: ſe dà principio, ou começa algum liuro, ou

lines.note: Explains that the word begins a book or introduces a subject. The grave in dà and the historical liuro are preserved.
Materia completes the explanation of an introductory discourse word. The scan has a continuous word, not provisional mate ia.
Soomot, with checked final t, is communal property, paraphrased soo no mono. The scan and supplied NINJAL headword support Sômot rather than OCR Bônos; the synonym also carries a circumflex.
Completes the definition as belonging to everyone. This clarifies that the preceding comunidade concerns collective ownership.
Somuqe is the verb for turning one's back; the Portuguese divides viradas across this row and the next. The q descender and the final hyphen are visible.
The example turns one's heart against a master, extending the physical action to disaffection. The lightly printed vowel after the long s is read as o, not the draft's u.

runs.text: Eſtar mal com o ſenhor, ou queixoſo delle.

lines.note: Iru completes the preceding Japanese example. The gloss means being on bad terms with one's lord, or resentful of him; the initial i is lowercase.

Somuqi introduces the intransitive verb meaning to go against or disobey; the Portuguese gives offending or breaking a rule. The printed stop after the headword is retained rather than regularized to a comma.

The example concerns disobeying a lord's will. Senhor continues on the next row; no additional end hyphen is supplied because the faint right-edge mark does not establish one against the aligned draft.

runs.text: nhor, ou a outra peßoa alta, & de reſpeito.

lines.note: This continues senhor and extends the gloss to another high-ranking, respected person. The printed joined double-s form in peßoa and the ampersand are preserved.
Fattouo identifies the law as the object of disobedience. The Portuguese explicitly says to break the law; the paragraph sign is apparatus, not part of the Japanese example.

Vôxeuo concerns a command, whose Portuguese explanation continues as mandado. The x is abraded but its remaining strokes and the repeated construction favor x over the draft's c; the circumflex on ô is retained.
The first phrase finishes the lord's command. The next example offers tenmei and ten as alternatives and divides somuqu at the printed hyphen; the joined Tenniſo- is not respaced editorially.
Muqu completes the preceding verb, glossed as offending God. A new example begins with the world as its object; the printed hyphen after Youo is retained.
The world example is glossed as despising the world. The next example begins dori, reason; the vowel is worn and no extra length mark is supplied beyond the aligned draft.
This completes dori ni somuqu, acting against reason. The scan supports ſomuqu rather than the malformed draft sequence, and the Portuguese retains its historical rezão spelling.
Son means loss or damage; son wo suru supplies the associated expression. The italic Vt introduces the upright Japanese example.
This short continuation translates the preceding son wo suru as suffering damage. It belongs to Son, not to the grammatical entry that follows.

runs.text: Particula que junta às raizes dos verbos,

lines.note: This begins the account of the verbal suffix sona, continued at the top of the right column. The headword's ending and accent are poorly inked: Sǒna is the preferred identification, also supported by the supplied NINJAL entry, but the caron cannot be established confidently from this impression. The legible gloss reads Particula que junta às raizes, not the garbled draft.

runs.text: ou a nomes ſignifica parecer, ou deuer ſer al-

lines.note: This continues Sǒna from the bottom of the left column: attached to verbs or nouns, it expresses seeming or being expected to be something. The row is indented as a continuation, and algũa begins at its end.
The example says that horse looks fast. The source has the sona suffix, not the draft's malformed xǒra ending; s and n are partly worn, while the length mark is a caron.
The horse gloss finishes here. The next example concerns a boat appearing about to depart; the thin tall character before ǒ is long ſ, not r.

runs.text: Parece q̃ ſe partirà a embarcação.

lines.note: Ni gozaru completes the boat example. The Portuguese predicts the vessel's departure and uses the unexpanded abbreviation q̃; the grave accent in partirà remains as printed.

runs.text: Como os outros, ou ẽ cõmũ cõ todos.

lines.note: Sônami is being like the others or on the same footing as everyone. The Portuguese abbreviation tildes are retained separately from the headword's circumflex.
This Sonata is the address to another person, glossed as you or your honor. The joined double-s form in voßa belongs to the italic Portuguese gloss.
The second Sonata is directional: over on that side. It is a separate homographic entry, not a repeated gloss for the preceding pronoun.

runs.text: Perto de vos, ou de voßa caſa.

lines.note: Adding atari gives the vicinity of the addressee or their house. The faint o of Sonata is retained, and the entire Portuguese explanation remains italic.
Sonauari concerns being endowed with or placed in a position. The supposed fer is ſer; the long s belongs to the Portuguese verb, and aleuãtado is divided across rows.
The example says that arts or accomplishments are possessed by a person. Ter begins the Portuguese translation and is kept wholly in the gloss typeface rather than splitting off its capital.

The first gloss is possessing arts and abilities in oneself. Curaini begins the next example, being installed in a rank; its worn u and n are clarified by the legible curaini repeated below at c2-l022, not by preserving the draft's malformed Ceraimi.
This completes sonauaru and translates it as being placed in a position of dignity. The broken word remains on two physical rows.
Sonaye is the transitive verb for offering or placing something before someone. The Portuguese por is the historical infinitive spelling, not an instruction to add a modern accent.

runs.text: couſa diãte de peßoa nobre, Fotoques, & c. Vt,

lines.note: Offerings may be set before a noble person or Buddhist sacred figures. Fotoques is a Japanese word embedded in the Portuguese explanation; the spaced & c. abbreviation is retained.
Xôranni introduces presenting something for sacred observation. The Portuguese gives showing or presenting; the long s in sonayuru is upright Japanese type, unlike the surrounding italic gloss.

This finishes the presentation to kami and Buddhist figures. The next example begins Go-: enlargement shows a worn capital G, whose detached right-hand stroke is not an extra r or i as the draft suggested.
Chiuo completes Go-chiuo, the food offering described by the Portuguese continuation. The line says to place or offer some food rather than introducing a new headword.
The food is placed before the kami. Miqiuo then introduces the drink offering; the Japanese verb is divided after sonayu-, while Cami remains within the Portuguese sentence.

The drink example is translated as setting wine before the kami. The next Japanese example begins with God in heaven; the raised nine-shaped abbreviation after De is represented by ꝰ without expansion, and the tilde in tẽni is retained.

Moon, sun, and stars are the objects of God's arranging them. The scan reads sonaye, not sonave; the mark over the final o of the honorific tamǒ is very faint, with a caron preferred on enlargement. The Portuguese repeats the same raised abbreviation sign after De.

runs.text: nos ceos a lũa, ſol, & eſtrelas por ordẽ, &c.

lines.note: The Portuguese says God placed moon, sun, and stars in the heavens in order. This resolves the draft's broken estelas and o dẽ; the final nasal abbreviation belongs to the e in ordẽ.
This example is installing someone in a position or rank. Curaini is legible here and helps identify the worn occurrence above; the tilde in alguẽ is not expanded.
The single word completes the preceding gloss about investing someone with dignity. It is body text and retains its own physical line and indentation.

This gives alternative forms for loss or destruction, with the Japanese explanation sonji horoburu. The first-vowel marks in Sõbǒ and Sõji are nasal tildes, not length carons; NINJAL independently identifies the contracted Sõbǒ form. The visibly distinct foroburu is separated from Sõji.
Sonbocu is an honorific designation for a letter from a noble person. The closing upright S is a register label rather than a continuation of the italic gloss.
Sonca refers to an honored conveyance, explained as a litter or coach. The worn first consonant of mono belongs to the Japanese phrase nori mono, not the draft's nono.

runs.text: chi de peßoa nobre, como Rey.

lines.note: Chi completes cochi, the coach belonging to a noble person such as a king. Rey is part of the Portuguese sentence; the final S is separately upright.
Soncacu is an honored guest, explained by tattoqi qiacujin. The two t types in Tattoqi are retained, correcting the draft's c confusion.
This continues the honored-guest gloss with and respected. It retains the ampersand and the separate final register label.

Soncan is another honorific term for a letter, also identified as gojǒ. The worn final n of the headword is preferred to the draft's punctuation fragment; the supplied NINJAL index corroborates the word, not its typography.
The continuation specifies that the letter comes from a noble person. It finishes Soncan rather than starting the village-official entry below.
Sonchǒ is the village head, paraphrased as the elder of the village. The Portuguese begins the description of the chief who governs a settlement.
The row completes the village-head definition: the person governing a settlement. The tilde is over u in algũa, and the historical pouoação spelling is retained.
Soncǒ is an honorific form of address to a lord. The gloss has Voßa, not Vaßa, and the title senhoria is physically divided after senho-.
This completes senhoria and lists excellency as another equivalent. The damaged middle of excellencia is treated as one word, not the draft's broken spacing.
Soncun denotes an honored lord. The Portuguese describes a good and honored lord: honrado is one adjective, not the draft's honra do; Bõ remains an unexpanded nasal abbreviation.
This is the noun for envy. Its faint m has not created a new word boundary; the historical Portuguese j in Enueja is preserved.

This is the related verb, to envy. The vowel between n and ô in the last principal form is severely worn: neôda is the preferred reading of the remaining lower stroke and agrees with the supplied NINJAL record, but noôda remains a visual alternative. The anomalous form is not normalized to an expected modern paradigm.

The Japanese example is envying a person. At the far right, the parenthesis and idade. S. belong physically to this row but complete the Sǒnen definition printed below; that displaced material is restored here without reflowing it into the following line.
Sǒnen is the vigorous or youthful age of life. The phrase ser da is completed by idade printed at the far right of the preceding physical row; the gloss's long ſ is not f.
Sǒnet is explained by dry and warm, not the draft's malformed asataca. Both Japanese gloss words are upright, and the Portuguese description continues below.
This completes dry and hot, then adds fever as another meaning. Item is italic Portuguese apparatus; the closing S is upright.
Songan is an honorific term for a person's face. The small final a of peßoa is very faint beside the right rule but is retained as the completion of the word, not replaced by the draft's stop.
The face belongs to an honored or noble person, a king, and so forth. The whole description is Portuguese, with a separate upright S label.
Songiǔ denotes revering or honoring, as shown by its two Japanese explanations. The faint right edge still supports Venerar; the scan does not call for a new line-end hyphen.

Reverence is directed especially toward Buddhist sacred figures. Principalmẽte has worn middle strokes and a nasal abbreviation; the following phrase is read Sõgiǔ, ſanda, with a tilde over the first o and a caron over u, although the latter and the n in ſanda are weak. This remains a qualified reading rather than an expansion of the Japanese phrase.

This translates the preceding phrase as venerating, praising, and magnifying Buddhist sacred figures. The heavily worn ẽgrãdecer is retained with its two nasal marks; Fotoques is embedded in the Portuguese gloss. The final S is faint and no unsupported terminal stop is supplied.
The worn catchword is read as Songǒ, matching the first headword on f0446. The caron is faint and no unsupported terminal stop is supplied.
